new_statements.quote: Le corse possède un accent tonique, qui assume une fonction contrastive, c’est-à-dire qui permet d’opposer entre elles des séquences identiques par ailleurs. Cet accent peut frapper la dernière syllabe (oxytons : [mat?in'a] « moudre »), l’avant-dernière syllabe (paroxytons : [mat?'ina] « il moud »), l’avant-avant-dernière syllabe (proparoxytons : [m'at?ina] « meule »). On peut également trouver des séquences dans lesquelles l’accent remonte sur la quatrième syllabe à compter de la fin ; mais ce schème est réservé aux cas dans lesquels le mot est suivi de deux enclitiques : [d'?timini] « donnez-m’en » s’analyse comme d'?ti + mi + ni.
new_statements.translation: Corsican has a tonic (word) stress with a contrastive function, i.e. it can distinguish sequences that are otherwise identical. This stress may fall on the last syllable (oxytones: [mat?in'a] 'to grind'), the penultimate (paroxytones: [mat?'ina] 'he grinds'), or the antepenultimate (proparoxytones: [m'at?ina] 'millstone'). One also finds sequences where the stress goes back to the fourth syllable from the end, but that pattern is restricted to cases where the word is followed by two enclitics: [d'?timini] 'give me some' = d'?ti + mi + ni.
new_statements.citation: Dalbera-Stefanaggi, Marie-José (2002). La langue corse. Paris: Presses Universitaires de France. 125 pp.
new_statements.locator: ch. III 'Caractéristiques linguistiques', section I 'Phonétique et phonologie', 1 'L'accentuation', p. 21 (opening paragraph; Cairn preview) — file also)

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (Comiti 1996 via InterRomania) codes Corsican as lexical with an empty rule but its quote already names the same three positions (oxytonic, paroxytonic, proparoxytonic); Dalbera-Stefanaggi agrees on type and adds that the stress is contrastive with a minimal triplet, the three-syllable window, and the enclitic-only fourth-from-last case; identical to the two existing statements held by the project (which come from this same preview).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is contrastive (lexical) and falls on one of the last three syllables (final, penultimate or antepenultimate); stress on the fourth-from-last occurs only when two enclitics follow the word (verb + mi + ni). The stressed vowel is lengthened, with intensity and pitch concentrated on its first part.

new_statements.exceptions: pre-antepenultimate stress only in verb + two enclitics sequences ([d'?timini] = d'?ti + mi + ni); the '?' in the IPA forms is Cairn's own HTML rendering of a character it could not display
new_statements.identity_note: Dalbera-Stefanaggi 2002 describes Corsican as a whole ('l'ensemble des variétés'), deferring regional variation to later chapters; Giudicelli 2006 (unopened) treats the Taravese variety of Chisa, southern Corsica.

tone.quote: In almost all cases, the F0 peak is located in the end of the question (the verb phrase) in Parisian French: on the penultimate or on the final vowel of the utterance. By contrast, in the majority of cases, the maximum F0 value is located in the beginning of the question in Corsican and Corsican French. ... In an autosegmental-metrical framework, the initial peak (which does not show a precise syllabic anchoring) could be analysed as a left peripheral high boundary tone (%H) and the final pattern as H+L* L-L%.

tone.quote: En corse, en revanche, les mots peuvent être oxytons, paroxytons ou proparoxytons, c’est-à-dire accentués sur la dernière syllabe, sur l’avant-dernière syllabe ou sur l’antépénultième, respectivement. ... Chez les bilingues, que ce soit en corse ou en français, on peut remarquer un ton haut en début de question (sans ancrage sur une syllabe précise), tandis que la syllabe accentuée de fin d’énoncé est réalisée avec une descente mélodique.
tone.locator: p. 611 (section 2, corpus design) and p. 612 (section 3 'Prosodie de questions corses/françaises')
tone.translation: In Corsican, by contrast, words can be oxytone, paroxytone or proparoxytone, i.e. stressed on the last, the penultimate or the antepenultimate syllable respectively. ... In the bilinguals, whether in Corsican or in French, one notices a high tone at the beginning of the question (not anchored to any particular syllable), while the stressed syllable at the end of the utterance is realised with a melodic fall.
tone.summary: No lexical tone (stress language); intonation: unanchored question-initial H + falling nuclear contour on final stressed syllable.

tone.says: Theses.fr abstract: description of the Cap Corse dialects from fieldwork and the ALF-Corse/ALEIC/NALC atlases; the phonetics chapter treats the evolution of the Latin consonants (little lenition, original consonant strengthening especially in s+consonant sequences) and the singular stressed-vowel system of Morsiglia (mid-open/mid-close vowels); then verb morphology, lexicon and dialect areas vs historical territories. Nothing on accent placement, prosody or tone in the abstract; no lexical tone…

sources.citation: Nesi, Annalisa. 1988. 284. Korsisch: Interne Sprachgeschichte / Evoluzione del sistema grammaticale, 799-808 [with 285. Marcellesi, Jean-Baptiste & Thiers, Jacques, Korsisch: Soziolinguistik / Sociolinguistique, 809-820, and 286. Giacomo-Marcellesi, Mathée, Korsisch: Externe Sprachgeschichte, 820-835]. In Günter Holtus, Michael Metzeltin & Christian Schmitt (eds.), Lexikon der Romanistischen Linguistik (LRL), Band IV: Italienisch, Korsisch, Sardisch / Italiano, Corso, Sardo. Tübingen: Niemeyer. xvi+935 pp. ISBN 3-484-50234-7 (De Gruyter e-book ISBN 978-3-11-096610-7, DOI 10.1515/9783110966107).
